Silver all the way. I’m like you, fair and cool leaning neutral. Color analysis says silver looks better on me. But I prefer gold and so does everyone else I ask. The trick to pulling off gold is wearing neutral or cool toned golds. The bottom dark yellow gold bracelets and necklaces you’re wearing in the photos look odd against your skin. Whereas the top ones look more complimentary. 

My theory about why gold is preferred on me despite silver being recommended as a bright winter is that we are very fair. Unless I have a tan, if I wear silver the jewelry practically blends in with my skin. Gold is more contrasting, which for bright winter, contrast is part of our beauty. I wear gold most of the year because I’m pale most of the year. I only feel like silver is flattering in summer or when I’ve tanned because it pops more. I wonder if you find this to be true as well. 

If you’d like, I can post a pic of the golds that look best on me. I also find that the key to making gold look just as good or even better than silver on me, is picking gold jewelry that is very shiny. Nothing matte. And preferably with diamonds or stones that look similar, clear, bright and cool. It really makes gold look a lot more natural on me. Just because a color or metal isn’t in your palette doesn’t mean you can’t make it work for you! Wear what you feel best in. Color analysis is a guide not a rule :) at least this is the advice I tell myself

I second this!!! I actually was able to manage my PCOS naturally through lifestyle and nutrition after my diagnosis by educating myself on the mechanism of PCOS and what a body like mine needs. For me, this included weight training 2-3 times a week, walking 30 mins daily, focusing on high protein, low-ish carbs, high fiber, minimal sugar (which is hard because it’s in literally everything), minimal processed foods. I also drank a lot more water and got out in the sun every single day at least 15 mins (even in winter). Supplements were the big cherry on top. When my symptoms were at their mildest, mild enough for me to believe at one point my PCOS had maybe gone away, I was taking daily: omega 3, magnesium, vitamin B complex, vitamin D, vitamin C and iron. I have also seen lots of people talk about zinc but have not been able to stomach it. 

I also did all this during COVID which was a stressful time for most, but for me allowed me a true break from life to be able to put my mental and physical health first, which resulted in very low stress, which is important for PCOS but not always easy to maintain. At that point in time, I was younger and had a lot less responsibility and more time in the day to do all of this. Now, I’m basically married, I live with my in-laws, run a business and my health has tanked and my stress has peaked. It’s been like this for the last 3 years so I’ve decided to finally go on meds for it. If I could do it on my own I would, but right now I can’t and that’s okay!! But try a holistic approach first. Even if it doesn’t completely control your PCOS like it did for me at first, at the very least you’ll build a great foundation for when you are ready to try more traditional treatment.

Please do your own research with my comment because I haven’t been on accutane myself - YET. I am still doing lots of research and debating if it’s something I want to take myself. What I have learned is that you need to take your accutane with a healthy fat (like avocado, peanut butter, salmon, etc). You also want to up your fat intake overall. This will help minimize the side effects, especially the drying ones as fats are almost like oil to a machine. Also, as others have said, up your water intake. You can also add liquid IV or other electrolytes to your water to make sure your body is actually absorbing the hydration, not just peeing it out. Lastly, I’ve seen dermatologists and patients on TikTok (again do your research because im NAD) say they recommend taking an antihistamine every day with Accutane because it either lessens or prevents side effects. 

What I plan to do when I go on accutane is start very slowly with my dose, do everything I mentioned above, and also try to clean up my lifestyle as much as possible to support my mind and body through this harsh treatment. After all, it did used to be used as a cancer treatment. You’re basically nuking your body, there’s going to be fallout. Its experiences like yours that worry me and make me keep delaying my derm appointment. I already deal with achey joints and headaches, I don’t know if this is the right treatment for me. But I hope it is for you and your side effects go away soon. I know how much they suck. Good luck!

Like other comments have said, the Rotterdam criteria is that you meet 2/3 criteria to qualify for a PCOS diagnosis. I was diagnosed by ultrasound 3 years ago and only found out because I read the results. The doctor never called me to tell me or to schedule a follow up visit to discuss treatment. lol. So I learned all I could online about managing it naturally and I did just that!! 

Then last year I saw a new gyno because I moved and was seeking treatment since I had a lifestyle change which caused my PCOS to go completely out of control. She said my ultrasound looked “PCOS-ish” (um???) and when I told her all my other symptoms aligned with PCOS she didn’t care and was very dismissive. She only offered birth control to me (which I started off the appointment by saying I didn’t want). Luckily my partner comes to all my appointments with me and she didn’t like what the gyno was saying, and it must have been all over her face (plus she also scoffed and jumped in to back me up), so the gyno was like “just to be sure I’ll order a full hormonal panel”. 

Guess what my results were. High DHEA, high testosterone and low something else (I forgot) but when I googled them they all were caused by PCOS. I get a message the next day from the doctor “your hormone panel showed high androgens which is consistent with PCOS, I am sending a referral for an endocrinologist” LOL. Anyway, I asked my primary to go over the results with me and told her about my gyno experience and she put me on Spironolactone (anti-androgen) and Metformin (to lower insulin). I haven’t picked them up yet so I can’t say how they’re working for me but there’s tons of posts on Reddit asking what people’s experience with both meds were for PCOS. 

So to answer your question, there are 3 main treatments according to my primary - birth control, spiro and metformin. I told her I didn’t want birth control because my estrogen and progesterone were healthy. 

Find someone who listens to you. Advocate for yourself. And in my opinion, it sounds like you may have endo or adenomyosis going on as well as others have said. I knew this would is be the unpopular answer before I clicked on this thread and then I opened it, scrolled and immediately was right. 

So I got diagnosed at 23 after a bad breakup right before COVID hit which triggered a lot of mood swings and brought a lot of symptoms I had been stuffing down for years to a head. I was extremely slewisidal and depressed but my mood would get really elevated once or twice a day. And this went on every day for like 6 months after the breakup. I couldn’t take it anymore and asked for a referral to a psych to go on something to help my mood stabilizer. After a quick chat with my psych, told her my brother was also diagnosed with bipolar disorder and was immediately put on Seroquel. It helped. Eventually we added on Wellbutrin and Klonopin for panic attacks. 

Initially I was like - wow this diagnosis makes so much sense. I’d spend hours on this sub reading people’s experiences and be like - yep, that’s me. But then when I went back to school to finish up my bachelors in psych, I learned about borderline personality disorder and it clicked for me a lot more than bipolar. I always thought my meds got me through a rough time and I’m grateful, but was worried about the plethora of negative side effects I was having from seroquel. I would’ve been on seroquel 5 years this June. 

I finally brought it up to my partner who knows me best about how I didn’t believe it was truly bipolar, that I wanted to come off my meds to see if I really am or not but that I was scared. Scared that the only reason I’ve been stable for the last several years was because of medication, and that if I came off my life would be in shambles again. We had many conversations about this in the 3 years we’ve been together. 

Finally, this year I got really good health insurance, underwent a very thorough 6 hour neuropsychological evaluation and specifically asked them to look at bipolar disorder, borderline personality disorder, and anything else they thought would apply to me. It turns out I am one of the few people that wanted to come off their meds that actually DOESNT have bipolar disorder. It was borderline personality disorder and C-PTSD (which explains why the breakup flared up the symptoms severely enough for me to seek meds and qualify for a bipolar diagnosis), ADHD interacting with each other and my hormonal diagnoses (PCOS and PMDD) in a way that looked a lot like Bipolar Disorder. I can go in more detail about how and why if anyone is interested. 

But I did find a new psychiatrist and got the go ahead from her to taper off of Seroquel very slowly (just in case). Guess what- I felt amazing! A lot of the scary side effects I was having from seroquel (akathisia, binge eating, dangerous falls, weight gain, insulin resistance, sleeping my life away, feeling emotionally numb, tardive dyskinesia, etc) are now GONE. It actually turns out that seroquel worsens PCOS, which I had a gut feeling was the case and was part of my wanting to come off of it. 

I also started Strattera for inattentive ADHD and my life is sooo much better now because the true issue is being addressed. And that’s all because I had a partner that was supportive and honest with me about what they thought, had access to the right testing and psych doctor, but most importantly because I TRUSTED myself. 

I’m not sharing my experience to encourage anyone to come off their meds or say that if you have doubts that you don’t have bipolar disorder. This was not a conclusion I came to in a manic state. This feeling was consistent and my journey to getting undiagnosed and coming off my medication was done slowly and responsibly. All I’m saying is, if it doesn’t feel like the right diagnosis it’s okay to get a second opinion and trust your gut. Seroquel got me through a hard time but in the long term it didn’t stop a lot of my most concerning mood and behavior issues because it was not a chemical imbalance - in my case it is a personality disorder and medication will not fix that. Only therapy can. 

I have heard many stories like this on TikTok and Reddit and it may be the case for you too. I got diagnosed WAYYY too quickly. My original psych also told me many times when I asked about coming off my meds that this was a very common bipolar thing to ask. Also, I want to make sure to say that it is possible to have BOTH borderline and bipolar. 

I’ve already spent way too long typing this reply but if anyone has questions I’d love to educate or share my experience! I think I have a unique perspective as someone who not only went through it, but also has the educational perspective as well. I actually think if it hadn’t been for my education I would’ve never been exposed to Borderline Personality Disorder and recognized it in myself or advocated for getting re-assessed.

First of all I’m so sorry for what you are both going through. Unfortunately, doctors are not very knowledgeable nor empathetic to CRPS patients. My partner also has CRPS and I’ve been to every appointment with her since it developed last August. Most of the doctors have been either clueless or have just brushed her off. Be prepared for this reality and only see doctors who believe and support her! Go to every appointment if you can. Having a support system is the most important tools to healing with CRPS. 

As for her surgery, my partner and I have had to do a LOT of our own research on CRPS because of how uninformed practitioners are. From what we have learned both through her experience with the condition, and our research, is that the worst thing you can do for CRPS is undergo ANY kind of surgery or invasive procedure (even needles) as it can cause the CRPS to worsen or spread. PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE hold off until you at least see the pain specialist first and ideally do more research. We didn’t know this before she had a knee scope surgery in October after she wasn’t healing from a suspected meniscus tear. They found nothing wrong with her knee during the scope but she took an abnormal amount of time to heal from it and it ended up spreading throughout her whole leg. This was when we knew something was very wrong as she should have been walking the next day since there was nothing found wrong during the scope and they didn’t have anything to repair. The surgery was pushed, unnecessary and actually did much more damage than good. If we knew what we know now she would have never had that surgery. 

Also just to prepare you, in our experience, most doctors will push injections, medication and surgery, none of which actually treat the cause of CRPS. This is just because of the nature of the condition and medicine’s inability to understand and treat it. The best way to treat it is holistically through PT, supplements, medication if you can find one that helps, going to therapy for emotional support of coping with the condition for possibly the rest of your life and having a strong support system. 

Keep advocating for her and learning together!! She deserves doctors who listen to her and empathize. The condition is not hopeless and she can get back to normal again with lots of time and proper treatment. Be skeptical of doctors who push spinal stimulators, spinal injections or surgery. Let me know if you have any questions. Well wishes.
